## Learning objectives

1.  Describe the basic energy fluctuation patterns of walking and running in terrestrial gaits, as approximated by spring-loaded inverted pendulum models

2.  Understand the basic principles of scaling with geometric similarity (or isometry), and state predictions for changes in strength and loading with increasing body size under the predictions of geometric similarity.

3.  State the dynamic similarity hypothesis, and be able to generate predictions for dimensionless quantities according to the predictions of dynamic similarity.

4.  Use an example data set on gait of running birds to investigate how stride length and stride frequency vary with size, and visualize how the variation collapses when data are normalized to dimensionless quantities.

## Overview

### Gait types and their mechanical signatures

The two primary gaits of striding bipeds — walking and running — differ in the dynamics of the body's center of mass and in foot-contact timing, summarized by the **duty factor** (stance duration divided by stride duration). When duty factor exceeds 0.5, double-support periods are present and the inverted-pendulum mechanism operates: the body vaults over a relatively stiff stance leg, exchanging gravitational potential and kinetic energy out of phase to reduce external mechanical work. When duty factor falls below 0.5, an aerial phase is present, the leg compresses like a spring during stance, and kinetic and potential energy fluctuate in phase; elastic energy storage in tendons and ligaments compensates for the loss of the pendulum exchange. Some birds also use a *grounded running* gait in which spring-like center-of-mass dynamics occur without a true aerial phase.

### Physical models for walking and running

The **spring-mass** (or spring-loaded inverted pendulum, SLIP) model represents a runner as a point mass supported by a single massless spring leg and captures ground-reaction-force magnitude and timing across a wide range of running animals and speeds. The single-leg inverted-pendulum model of walking predicts a smooth single-humped vertical force profile, whereas measured walking forces show a characteristic double-humped, M-shaped profile; Geyer, Seyfarth, and Blickhan (2006) resolved this by extending the spring-mass model to two legs, demonstrating that both walking and running can be understood within the same SLIP framework. The SLIP model has since become the standard template model for studying legged locomotion dynamics across species.

### Geometric similarity and the scaling challenge

**Isometric scaling** (geometric similarity) describes what happens to lengths, areas, and volumes when an animal is scaled up without changing shape: if linear dimensions scale by some factor, cross-sectional areas scale as the square and volumes (and body mass, at constant density) scale as the cube. Because muscular and skeletal strength is proportional to cross-sectional area while body weight scales as volume, larger animals are relatively weaker under geometric similarity. To compensate, larger animals tend to adopt a more upright, straighter-legged posture that orients the skeleton more vertically and reduces the muscular force required to support body weight in stance.

### The dynamic similarity hypothesis

Alexander and Jayes (1983) proposed the **dynamic similarity hypothesis**: animals of different sizes use mechanically equivalent gaits when their dimensionless gait parameters — normalized by an appropriate set of characteristic physical quantities — are equal. This is both a theoretical prediction and an empirically testable hypothesis; if locomotor function scales in a dynamically similar manner, size-related differences in absolute gait measures should disappear once expressed as dimensionless quantities, and deviations from this collapse reveal genuine functional differences across size.

### Dimensionless quantities for locomotion analysis

The governing physical parameters of the SLIP — body mass (*M*), leg length (*L*), and gravitational acceleration (*g*) — provide the base quantities for normalizing all gait variables to dimensionless form.

| Quantity | Dimensionless form |
|---|---|
| Length / distance | Divide by *L* |
| Force | Divide by *Mg* |
| Time | Divide by $\sqrt{L/g}$ (pendular period) |
| Frequency | Multiply by $\sqrt{L/g}$ |
| Speed | Divide by $\sqrt{gL}$ |
| Energy / work | Divide by *MgL* |

McMahon and Cheng (1990) applied this normalizing framework to the spring-mass running model, formalizing dimensionless parameters for running mechanics including dimensionless leg stiffness, dimensionless peak force, and dimensionless speed. A particularly important dimensionless quantity is the **Froude number** (Fr = V²/gL): when Fr = 1, the centripetal acceleration required to maintain ground contact during the arc of stance equals gravitational acceleration, and purely inverted-pendulum walking becomes physically impossible; measured walk-to-run transitions in many animals occur near this limit, supporting the Froude number as a dimensionless speed benchmark for gait transitions.

### Scaling patterns in avian bipedal locomotion

A dataset spanning a 2,500-fold range in body mass — from painted quail to ostriches, drawn from 21 species in the literature — provides a rigorous cross-species test of dynamic similarity in avian bipedal locomotion (Daley & Birn-Jeffery 2018). In absolute units, large birds operate at lower stride frequencies and longer strides than small birds; after normalization to dimensionless quantities, large birds use relatively higher dimensionless stride frequencies and relatively shorter dimensionless stride lengths — the inverse of the absolute rank order. This reflects a more vertically bouncy center-of-mass trajectory in large birds, associated with reduced fore-aft ground-reaction-force fluctuations and lower mechanical work demand per stride.

### Practical considerations for cross-species and cross-population comparisons

Several analytical choices affect the validity of dimensionless normalization and should be made deliberately. **Leg length** is most commonly measured as standing hip height, which approximates resting leg length and is consistent across species, but grows faster than skeletal segment length with body mass because larger animals stand more upright; the sum of limb-segment lengths or segment lengths back-calculated under isometric scaling may be more appropriate depending on the task. Whether to include the foot depends on how the animal contacts the ground during the task of interest: the effective leg length is the distance from the center of mass to the point of ground contact, whatever the anatomy in between, and this principle applies equally when extending scaling analyses to individuals with atypical anatomy such as para-athletes or individuals with limb differences. Measuring comparable speed ranges across species also requires care, as laboratory-elicited speeds may not represent true maximum effort in all species.
